981.title: Dalit Christians
981.hook: Indian Christians from communities once called untouchable
981.howItsDone: Dalit Christian communities in India worship in their own congregations and in mixed ones, and churches and Dalit theologians have taken up the fight against caste discrimination, including within the church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Christians of the Middle East, praying where the name was first spoken. Your line was the oldest churches. Which one did you look up, and what did you learn? Day nine hundred eighty-one.

Who is allowed to touch whom? Societies keep quiet rules about it, and children pick them up early. In Mark's Gospel a man with a skin disease, a leper, kneels in the road in front of Jesus. By the custom of the day, people kept their distance from him, and he kept his from them. He says, if you want to, you can make me clean. And before Jesus says a word in reply, he does what everyone else had been careful not to do. He reaches out and touches him. Today, Dalit Christians, and that touch.

In India, caste has divided people for a long time, and at the bottom of that order were communities treated as untouchable: people kept from wells, from temples, from the tables of others. Dalit is a name people from these communities use for themselves today. Among India's Christians are Dalit families, and their story matters. Some of them heard their own story in that leper on the road. Mark tells it like this, in the King James Bible: "And Jesus, moved with compassion, put forth his hand, and touched him, and saith unto him, I will; be thou clean." Touch first, then words. Paul wrote something just as plain: "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus." But caste did not stop at the church door. Dalit Christians and church leaders in India have spoken about separate seating, separate cemeteries, and pulpits closed to them in some places, inside the church itself. So some Dalit Christian thinkers read the Bible from where they stood, and called it Dalit theology. They noticed that Jesus himself was pushed out, and they read Isaiah's line about the servant as their own: "He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief." On that reading, God is not at the top of the ladder looking down. God is with the ones the ladder left out. Churches in India are still working out what that asks of them.
screen: `HE PUT FORTH HIS HAND, AND TOUCHED HIM.`
`CASTE DID NOT STOP AT THE CHURCH DOOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the person you look past. Settle, and breathe. Think through your week. Who do you see often but never really greet? The person who cleans the office. The one who brings your packages. The relative everyone talks over at dinner. Pick one face. Do you know their name? If not, notice that. Now hold them in mind with the respect you'd give someone you admire. If you pray, you can pray for them by name, or by face if that's all you have. If you don't, simply wish them well, and plan how you'll greet them next time. The bell holds the time.
Dalit Christians. Indian Christians from communities once treated as untouchable, and a theology that reads the Gospel from the bottom of the ladder.
Your line: no one untouchable. Today, honor someone's dignity on purpose: learn a name, offer a hand, or make room at a table. Day nine hundred eighty-one.

he "put forth his hand, and touched him" first.

options: heals him with a word from a safe distance.
reaches out and touches him.

fork.reveal: "Jesus, moved with compassion, put forth his hand, and touched him." the touch comes before the healing words.

what it means: Christians from communities once treated as untouchable, who still face caste prejudice, sometimes even in church.
what a scholar hears: Dalit theology, reading Mark's touch and Isaiah's despised servant from the bottom of the caste order.

982.title: Pacific Christianity
982.hook: from Fiji to Samoa, village churches fill with harmony on Sunday
982.howItsDone: In Pacific island churches, Sunday worship is often marked by full congregational and choir singing in several parts, frequently without instruments, and in some island villages Sunday itself is kept as a day of rest.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dalit Christians, and a hand that reached out on the road. Your line was no one untouchable. Whose name did you learn, or whose hand did you take? Day nine hundred eighty-two.

Sunday morning, a village on a Pacific island. The shops are shut. The road is quiet. Then, from a white church near the water, the singing starts. No organ. No screen with the words. Just voices, men low, women high, parts weaving over and under each other, so full the windows seem to hum. A visitor stands outside and doesn't want to go in, in case it stops. In Samoa, in Tonga, in Fiji, Sunday has a sound. Today, Pacific Christianity, and the choir.

The gospel came to the Pacific by ship, with missionaries from Britain and elsewhere. That story has its hard chapters, as mission stories often do, tangled with trade and empire. But it did not stay a foreign thing. Islanders themselves became the teachers and pastors, and some sailed on to other islands, carrying the faith in their own languages. Some island readers find their place already named in the Psalms. In the King James Bible: "The LORD reigneth; let the earth rejoice; let the multitude of isles be glad thereof." The multitude of isles. Isaiah says it too: "Sing unto the LORD a new song, and his praise from the end of the earth, ye that go down to the sea, and all that is therein; the isles, and the inhabitants thereof." Islands at the end of the earth, singing. Hymns arrived with the missionaries, and island singers took them somewhere new, folding in their own ways of singing in many parts at once. A Tongan or Samoan choir doesn't just perform a hymn. It builds one, voice by voice. And that's the quiet lesson inside harmony. In unison, everyone sings the same note. In harmony, everyone sings a different note, and the notes fit. No one voice carries the song alone; if the basses drop out, everyone hears the hole. The letter to the Colossians tells an early church to be "teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord." One another. Singing, in that letter, is something a church does together, not something it watches.
screen: `LET THE MULTITUDE OF ISLES BE GLAD.`
`A CHOIR BUILDS A HYMN, VOICE BY VOICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your part. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a hymn or any song you know well, one that has carried you somewhere. Hum the first line, quietly, low in your chest. Then hum it again and listen to the room around you, the hum of the fridge, traffic, a bird, and notice how your note sits among them. You are one part of a larger sound. If you pray, you can let the humming be your prayer, or say the psalm's line: let the multitude of isles be glad. If you don't, simply keep humming, and listen. The bell holds the time.
Pacific Christianity. The faith of Fiji, Samoa, Tonga and the islands around them, carried island to island by islanders, and sung in many parts at once.
Your line: the island choirs. Today, sing in harmony with someone: in the car, at the sink, at bedtime. Take the low part or the high part, but don't take the same one. Day nine hundred eighty-two.

983.title: The Orthodox revival
983.hook: after communism, churches rebuilt across Eastern Europe
983.howItsDone: In Orthodox churches, worshipers usually stand, light candles before icons, kiss them and cross themselves, and the Divine Liturgy is sung, often with no instruments, across Russia, Ukraine, Romania, Greece, Georgia and beyond.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pacific Christianity, and a village church so full of voices the windows hummed. Your line was the island choirs. Did you find someone to sing with, and which part did you take? Day nine hundred eighty-three.

In the middle of Moscow there was once a great white cathedral with golden domes. Under Stalin's government it was blown up. For years the site held a hole in the ground, and then an open-air swimming pool, steaming in the winter cold. People swam laps where the altar had been. Then the government that built the pool was gone, and the cathedral was rebuilt on the same spot, dome by dome. Today, the Orthodox revival, and what it means to build again.
screen: `A SWIMMING POOL WHERE THE ALTAR WAS.`

segments.voice: That cathedral is one story among smaller ones like it. Across Russia, Ukraine, Romania, Bulgaria, Georgia and their neighbors, communist governments had closed churches, or turned them into warehouses, museums, cinemas, even stables. When those governments fell, the churches came back. Bells were recast. Icons came out of hiding. Monasteries that had stood empty took in monks and nuns again. Grown adults lined up to be baptized. The Bible has a scene that sounds like this. When exiles came home to Jerusalem, the book of Ezra says, they laid the foundation of a new temple, and the old men who remembered the first one wept with a loud voice, "and many shouted aloud for joy." Then this line, in the King James Bible: "the people could not discern the noise of the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping of the people." That's what rebuilding sounds like. Joy and grief at the same time, so mixed you can't pull them apart. Rebuilding stirs questions too. People inside and outside these churches have argued about how close a rebuilt church should stand to a government, and Orthodox Christians themselves hold different views on it. Walls can be raised with money and stone. Teaching a generation that had never been inside how to stand before an icon, light a candle and pray takes longer. In Nehemiah, the people look at the ruined walls and say, "Let us rise up and build."
screen: `THE SHOUT OF JOY AND THE WEEPING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: step inside. If there's an Orthodox church near you, you can visit one this week; if not, picture one now. Settle, and breathe. The door is heavy. Inside it smells of beeswax and incense. There are few pews or none; people stand. In front of you is a wall of icons, faces of Christ, Mary and the saints, lit by thin candles in a tray of sand. Someone old lights a candle and crosses herself. Someone young watches how she does it. Stay in that room. If you pray, you can pray there for the churches that were rebuilt. If you don't, simply stand and look. The bell holds the time.
The Orthodox revival. Across Eastern Europe, after communism, churches reopened and rebuilt, bells recast, icons returned, and a new generation learned how to pray in them.
Your line: rebuilt. Today, find one thing in your life that was knocked down, a friendship, a habit, a hope, and lay one stone toward building it again. Day nine hundred eighty-three.

984.title: Big churches and house churches
984.hook: Christians gather in stadiums and in living rooms
984.howItsDone: Christians gather in congregations of every size, from large churches with several services each weekend to small groups meeting in homes, and some large churches organize their members into weekly home groups for prayer and Bible study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Orthodox revival, and a cathedral rebuilt where a swimming pool had been. Your line was rebuilt. What stone did you lay? Day nine hundred eighty-four.

Three thousand. Then, two or three. Both numbers are in the New Testament, and both describe a church. On a Sunday you can find each shape. An arena: a full parking lot, a band on a stage, lyrics on screens the size of houses, a crowd you can't see the end of. And a living room: a sagging couch, two kitchen chairs, a pot of soup on the stove for after. Someone reads a psalm. Someone else admits a hard week. The people in both rooms would call it church. Today, big churches and house churches.

Big or small? The question goes back to the church's earliest pages, and the Bible doesn't pick a side. In Acts, on the day of Pentecost, Peter preaches to a crowd in Jerusalem, and in the King James Bible: "the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls." A crowd, in a single day. But a few lines later, here's how those same people lived: "continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart." The temple courts and the kitchen table, both, daily. When Paul writes his letters, he sends greetings to churches that meet in people's homes: "Likewise greet the church that is in their house." The Greek word behind church, ekklesia, means an assembly, a gathering. It fits a crowd, and it fits a couch. Today the two shapes live side by side. Big churches can put on worship that lifts a whole arena, run food banks, and give a newcomer a seat where nobody notices them yet. House churches can know every name, notice who's missing, and carry each other's groceries. Each has its critics, and its defenders, and some big churches split into small home groups during the week to get both. Under all of it sits a promise Jesus made in Matthew about the smallest gathering of all: "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." Two or three. Read that way, God doesn't wait for a crowd.
screen: `IN THE TEMPLE, AND FROM HOUSE TO HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: gather your two or three. If someone is with you right now, you can do this together. If not, do it in your mind. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind two or three people you would want in that living room. Not the impressive ones. The ones you'd let see a hard week. Picture them on the couch. Notice who came to mind first, and who you're surprised to miss. If you pray, you can pray for each of them by name, or pray with them later, even by phone. If you don't, simply hold them, one at a time, with good will. The bell holds the time.
Big churches and house churches. Christians gather in arenas and in living rooms, and the New Testament has both: thousands in Jerusalem, and a church in someone's house.
screen: `BIG CHURCHES AND HOUSE CHURCHES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: where two or three. Today, gather two or three, for a meal, a walk, a call, and if you pray, pray together, even briefly. Day nine hundred eighty-four.

985.title: New communities
985.hook: Iona, Taizé, Bose and others: new monastic communities of mixed traditions
985.howItsDone: Visitors to Taizé, Iona and similar communities join the community's daily rhythm of common prayer, meals and work, and Taizé-style prayer, with short chants sung over and over, is held in parishes of different churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, big churches and house churches, an arena and a pot of soup. Your line was where two or three. Who were your two or three, and did you gather? Day nine hundred eighty-five.

A small island off the west coast of Scotland. The wind never quite stops. Beside an old abbey church stand the ruins of the buildings where monks once lived, roofless, grass growing inside the walls. Then a Scottish minister named George MacLeod arrives with a crew: young ministers in training and out-of-work stonemasons and carpenters, side by side. They live together, eat together, pray together morning and evening, and rebuild the ruins, stone by stone. Out of that work came the Iona Community. Today, new communities, and old ways for new people.

These new communities borrowed the old monastic shape and opened the doors to Christians of more than one church. Iona's members are scattered in ordinary jobs and homes, and they keep a shared rule of prayer, money and action for justice. In a village in France, a Swiss Protestant called Brother Roger began a community at Taizé, and brothers from Catholic and Protestant backgrounds joined him. Young people began to arrive from across Europe to stay a week, and Taizé gave them a way of praying anyone can join: short lines from scripture, sung over and over, until the words sing themselves. In Italy, at Bose, a community of men and women from different churches gathered to live by prayer, work and hospitality. None of these asks anyone to give up their own church. They ask for something older: life in common. The book of Acts describes the first believers like this, in the King James Bible: "And the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul: neither said any of them that ought of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common." All things common. And a psalm sings what that feels like from the inside: "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!" These communities have their own struggles; living together is hard, and their members say so. But each one took the ancient habits, set hours of prayer, shared meals, shared work, a guest always welcome, and handed them to people who never expected to become monks.
screen: `THE OLD SHAPE, WITH THE DOORS OPEN.`
`TAIZÉ: SHORT LINES, SUNG OVER AND OVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray the Taizé way, with an old line. Settle, and breathe. Take the psalm: behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity. Say it slowly, once. Then again. Then again, softer, letting the breath set the pace. If a different short line from scripture suits you better, use that. Don't push for meaning. Just let the repetition carry you, the way a room of young people at Taizé lets one line rise and fall. If you don't pray, simply repeat the words as a wish for the people you live and work with. The bell holds the time.
New communities. Iona, Taizé, Bose and others: communities that took the old monastic habits of prayer, work and shared life and opened them to Christians of different churches.

Your line: old ways, new people. Today, learn about one of these communities, Iona, Taizé or Bose, and borrow one of its habits: a set hour of prayer, a shared meal, or a guest made welcome. Day nine hundred eighty-five.

986.title: Five hundred years together (2016)
986.hook: Lutherans and Catholics mark the Reformation's anniversary by praying together in Lund
986.howItsDone: Catholics and Lutherans hold joint services of prayer in some places, using a common order of worship prepared for the Reformation commemoration, with thanksgiving, confession and commitment to unity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, new communities, Iona, Taizé and Bose, where Christians of different churches share one roof. Your line was old ways, new people. Which old habit did you borrow? Day nine hundred eighty-six.

A Lutheran cathedral in Lund, a city in the south of Sweden. At the front stand the pope, dressed in white, and the leaders of the Lutheran World Federation. They are there to mark an anniversary: the Reformation, the break that sent Catholics and Lutherans down separate roads, often against each other, sometimes in blood. A strange thing to commemorate together. And yet they've come to pray, in one service, from one book. Today, five hundred years together.

Tradition says the Reformation began when a monk named Martin Luther posted his arguments on a church door in Wittenberg. What followed was division, and much worse: wars, burnings and generations of suspicion on both sides. Past anniversaries had been kept apart, by one side without the other. Lund was different. Before it, Catholic and Lutheran theologians had worked through their history together and published a report with a title that became today's line: From Conflict to Communion. They had already agreed on a joint statement on justification, how a person is made right with God, the very question Luther had fought over. So the service at Lund did three things. It gave thanks for gifts each side had received through the Reformation. It confessed, out loud, the harm each side had done to the other. And it made promises: to keep praying together, to work together for the poor, to seek full unity. The pope and the Lutheran leaders signed a joint statement there. One honest note in it: Catholics and Lutherans still do not share communion at one table, and the statement named that as a pain they long to heal. Behind it all stands a prayer of Jesus in John's Gospel, on the night before he died, asking for his followers, in the King James Bible: "That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us." Paul has his own picture: "the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee." Lund didn't end the division. It turned the two sides around to face each other.
screen: `A DOOR IN WITTENBERG, AND A LONG DIVISION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring another church into the room. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who is a Christian of a different kind than the one you know best. Catholic, Lutheran, Orthodox, Baptist, Pentecostal, whatever is different for you. If you aren't a Christian, think of someone whose faith you don't share. Picture their face. Now think of one gift you have received through them or their tradition. Then one thing you might owe them an apology for, or simply one assumption you've made. If you pray, you can pray Jesus's line from John: that they all may be one. If you don't, simply wish them well. The bell holds the time.
Five hundred years together. Catholics and Lutherans marking the Reformation's anniversary at Lund, in one service of thanks, confession and promise.
Your line: from conflict to communion. Today, pray with someone from another church, or if that isn't possible, ask one of them what their church gave them, and listen. Day nine hundred eighty-six.

987.title: Care for our common home
987.hook: Pope Francis and Patriarch Bartholomew, with Protestant leaders, call Christians to care for creation
987.tomorrow: The priest and the big bang
987.howItsDone: Some churches keep a season of prayer for creation, and congregations take it up in different ways: services, planting, cleanups, and changes to how their buildings use energy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, five hundred years together: Lutherans and Catholics praying side by side in Lund. Your line was from conflict to communion. Who from another church did you pray with, or think of? Day nine hundred eighty-seven.

A pope writes a long letter, and he doesn't open it with a line of theology. He opens it with a song. An old Italian song by Francis of Assisi, praising God for the sun and the wind and the water, and for the earth, which Francis calls our sister and our mother. Pope Francis took that saint's name. Now he takes the saint's song and makes it the first words of a letter about the planet. And he isn't alone. The Orthodox patriarch Bartholomew, in Constantinople, has said plainly that harming the creation is a sin. Protestant and Anglican leaders have joined their voices too. Different branches of the church, on one subject. Today, care for our common home.
screen: `A LETTER THAT OPENS WITH A SONG.`

segments.voice: The phrase our common home is the subtitle of that letter, which takes its name from the song's opening words, Laudato si', praise be to you. The idea underneath it is very old. In the second chapter of Genesis, in the King James Bible: "And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it." Dress it and keep it. The man is a gardener before he is anything else. And keep is a strong word in this story. A chapter later, God sets cherubims at the garden's east side "to keep the way of the tree of life." Keeping, here, is guarding. And the Psalms say whose garden it is: "The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein." On that reading, the people living on the earth are tenants, not owners, and that is the thread running through what these church leaders say. Pope Francis writes that the cry of the earth and the cry of the poor are bound together, because when land and water are spoiled, the poorest feel it first. Patriarch Bartholomew speaks of the world as something to be received with thanks and offered back, the way bread is offered at the altar. Protestant leaders, in their own words, talk about stewardship: looking after what belongs to someone else. Christians still argue, honestly, about the details: what to do, how fast, who should pay. The letters don't settle those arguments. What they share is the starting point. The garden was handed over to be kept, not used up.
screen: `TO DRESS IT AND TO KEEP IT.`
`THE CRY OF THE EARTH AND OF THE POOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one thing for the earth. Settle, and breathe. Look around wherever you are. A tap, a light, a bin, a window, a patch of ground outside. Let your eye land on one ordinary thing you could look after a little better today. Turning something off. Picking something up. Fixing a drip. Keep it small enough that you will actually do it. If you pray, you can give thanks for the earth in the words of the psalm: the earth is the Lord's. If you don't, simply hold the thing you chose in mind, and let the two minutes be about keeping, not using. The bell holds the time.
Care for our common home. The subtitle of Pope Francis's letter on creation, and a call Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant leaders have made together: the earth is a garden to keep.

the Orthodox patriarch Bartholomew and Protestant and Anglican leaders have spoken too.
in Genesis, the man is put in the garden to own it

fork.setup: in Genesis 2, God takes the man and puts him in the garden of Eden. what is he there to do?
options: to use it up however he likes.
to dress it and to keep it.
to leave it untouched.
fork.reveal: "to dress it and to keep it." before anything else in the story, the man is a gardener, looking after ground that isn't his.

original.note: Hebrew: to keep, guard, watch over — the root of "to keep it" in Genesis 2:15.

trapdoor: what you thought: a modern slogan about recycling.
what it means: Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant leaders calling Christians to keep the earth as God's garden.
what a scholar hears: Genesis 2:15 read beside Genesis 3:24, where the same English word, keep, means guarding the way to the tree of life.
